summary: A first-principles tensor-network simulation of circuit QED dispersive readout captures the full unitary dynamics of a qubit and resonator coupled to a microscopic bath with arbitrary spectral density, avoiding standard Lindblad approximations. The study reveals that the qubit energy relaxation time $T_1$ can either decrease or increase with readout drive amplitude ($n̄$ photons) depending sensitively on the bath spectral function, with a Purcell notch filter at $ω_q$ producing qualitatively different behavior ($T_1$ increases with $n̄$) than Ohmic or flat spectra, contradicting predictions from simple Lindblad master equations.
motivation: Dispersive readout fidelity in superconducting qubits saturates or drops beyond certain drive amplitudes, accompanied by unexpected changes in $T_1$—a phenomenon not captured by standard phenomenological master equations. Understanding this effect requires a microscopic model of the measurement transmission line's frequency-dependent coupling to the system.
method: The authors simulate the time evolution of the circuit QED Hamiltonian (qubit at $ω_q/2π = 5.304$ GHz, resonator at $ω_a/2π = 7.5$ GHz, coupling $g/2π = 0.3165$ GHz) linearly coupled to a bath described by spectral density $J(ω)$, using tensor-network time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) with matrix-product states to evolve the full wavefunction. They extract qubit relaxation rates $Γ_{10}(n̄)$ by fitting exponential decay of $⟨Σ_z(t)⟩$ and reconstruct bath mode occupations $⟨n̂_ω⟩$ to perform frequency-resolved spectroscopy.
result: For an Ohmic spectrum with $J(ω) ∝ ω$ and Purcell filter depth $D = 0.7$, $σ = 0.1$ at $ω_q$, the normalized relaxation rate $Γ_{10}(n̄)/Γ_{10}(0)$ increases monotonically with photon number when the filter suppresses $J(ω_q)$, whereas for unfiltered Ohmic and flat spectra it decreases. The Lindblad model (Eq. 7) with single-photon dissipator predicts only monotonic decrease, failing qualitatively in the filtered case; agreement with microscopic Fermi's Golden Rule predictions (Eq. 22) confirms the importance of counter-rotating terms and spectral function evaluation at $ω_q$ rather than $ω_a$.
